Amit Shah Flags Off Bharat Forge Rifles for UP Special Task Force
morning.text:
Bharat Forge has flagged off its first lot of 5.56×45mm rifles made under an order from the Uttar Pradesh Special Task Force (UPSTF). Union Home Minister Amit Shah flagged off the shipment during his visit to Bharat Forge’s Kalyani unit in Pune on November 15.
The company said in a statement issued on November 16 that while inaugurating the 60th anniversary plaque, Shah was welcomed by Baba Kalyani, Chairman and Managing Director of Bharat Forge and took a tour of its manufacturing processes.
Shah was taken through a display of various defence products made and developed by Bharat Forge’s wholly-owned defence unit Kalyani Strategic Systems Limited (KSSL). This included small arms, artillery, ammunition and Unmanned Platforms for air, land and sea.
This shipment shows how domestic private sector manufacturers are playing an increasing part in supplying small arms to domestic security forces. The 5.56×45mm round is commonly used in modern military and police rifles.
However, Bharat Forge have not given any details about the model of rifle they have supplied, how many guns were ordered by the UPSTF, the value of the contract or how many rifles will be delivered. This proves they have shipped the first lot, but there is not enough information to know how big the order was.
It should also be noted that Bharat Forge have a separate contract with the Ministry of Defence for 255,128 Close Quarter Battle (CQB) Carbines. The contract worth ₹1,661.9 crore was signed in December 2025. The contract is with the Indian Army and involves a rifle developed jointly between Bharat Forge and the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s Armament Research and Development Establishment (ARDE).
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

morning.title: IAF Expects First Tejas Mk1A Squadron by March 2027
morning.text:
The Indian Air Force will start inducting the LCA Tejas Mk1A in the coming weeks and complete the induction of one full squadron before the end of the financial year, Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said, giving the clearest clues so far about how soon the IAF will induct the delayed fighter jet.
“Very shortly, we will have LCA Mark 1A joining the Indian Air Force; within this financial year we will have a squadron.” Within this financial year we will have a squadron inducted, Air Chief said at the ANI National Security Summit 3.0 in New Delhi on November 16.
The IAF had found four areas where the aircraft needed to be upgraded and hence worked closely with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) to upgrade it to the improved Mk1A configuration, Dixit said.
“We have completed almost all the four aspects. But then we also added some extra integration and testing because DRDO had developed new weapons for us,” he said.
The upgraded version of the fighter, the Mk1A, includes upgrades to the avionics, radar, electronic warfare systems and improved maintainability. It will have an active electronically scanned array radar, improved electronic warfare suite and have provisions to carry a larger variety of precision guided weapons. This makes it a much more capable aircraft than the initial Tejas Mk1.
But there is still a problem to overcome as the aircraft are moved from production and testing to actual deliveries. The programme has been delayed due to issues with the availability of the GE F404-IN20 engines.
However, Dixit isn’t saying they will get one full squadron delivered. Instead the aircraft will have to be delivered in batches and then accepted by the IAF and converted. The Air Chief wants one squadron by March 31, 2027.

morning.title: IG Defence Bets Big on Indigenous Micro-Missiles With Andhra Pradesh Complex
morning.text:
In a significant move to strengthen India’s strategic defence capabilities and indigenous missile manufacturing ecosystem, IG Defence has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Government of Andhra Pradesh in the presence of Hon’ble IT Minister of Andhra Pradesh, Shri Nara Lokesh & Hon’ble Union Minister of Civil Aviation Kinjarapu Ram Mohan Naidu, to establish a proposed 200-acre next-generation Missile Development and Manufacturing Complex in the state
The proposed complex will be dedicated to indigenous missile development, micro-missile technologies, propulsion systems, precision-strike capabilities and advanced defence manufacturing. The facility is envisioned as an integrated defence technology and industrial ecosystem, designed to support India’s growing requirements for domestically developed and manufactured defence systems.
Modern warfare is fundamentally reshaping defence preparedness. Recent conflicts, particularly across West Asia, have exposed the massive consumption of missiles, precision-guided munitions, interceptors and unmanned systems. Concerns over US munitions inventories and industrial capacity reinforce a critical lesson: military strength depends not just on advanced weaponry, but also on magazine depth, ammunition availability and the ability to replenish at scale. For India, this makes indigenous design, development, manufacturing and sustained replenishment capabilities essential to long-term defence preparedness
India’s future defence capabilities will depend not only on technological superiority but also on manufacturing sovereignty, resilient supply chains and the capacity to rapidly expand production in response to evolving security requirements. Against this backdrop, IG Defence’s proposed manufacturing complex represents an ambitious step towards building an indigenous industrial foundation for India’s next generation of missile and precision-strike technologies.
At the centre of IG Defence’s missile technology roadmap is JWALA™️, its indigenous next-generation micro-missile programme, aimed at advancing compact missile technologies and addressing emerging requirements in precision engagement and counter-unmanned aerial systems. As modern battlefields increasingly witness the deployment of low-cost drones, autonomous aerial platforms and increasingly sophisticated, unmanned threats, the demand for scalable, cost-conscious and technologically advanced missile solutions is growing. JWALA reflects IG Defence’s ambition to contribute to this evolving defence landscape through indigenous missile engineering and domestic manufacturing capabilities.
The programme has already achieved an important development milestone, with its solid rocket motors successfully test-fired, marking progress in the company’s indigenous propulsion development efforts.
The proposed Nellore complex will strengthen IG Defence’s long-term missile development and manufacturing ambitions, building indigenous capabilities across critical defence technology domains. At its core will be GRID Forge, IG Defence’s software-defined manufacturing system, digitally integrating production infrastructure, engineering, quality systems and industrial workflows. Designed to move beyond conventional factory infrastructure, GRID Forge will enable manufacturing visibility, process standardisation, production traceability, quality assurance and operational coordination. By combining intelligent software with advanced production infrastructure, IG Defence aims to create a scalable, future-ready and replicable defence manufacturing ecosystem, strengthening India’s ability to develop and manufacture critical defence technologies domestically.
The proposed complex will strengthen Andhra Pradesh’s growing aerospace and defence ecosystem by adding significant missile development and manufacturing capabilities. With strategic manufacturing clusters spanning naval systems in Visakhapatnam, missiles and ammunition, unmanned systems in Kurnool–Orvakal, and aerospace and electronics, the state is emerging as a key defence manufacturing hub. The proposed 200-acre IG Defence complex in Nellore will complement this ecosystem and strengthen indigenous defence supply chains. Under the MoU, APEDB will facilitate the investment process and coordinate with relevant government departments for project development, approvals and statutory clearances. Commenting on the development, Bodhisattwa Sanghapriya, Founder and CEO of IG Defence, said:
“Modern warfare is no longer defined by technology alone. It is equally defined by how quickly a nation can manufacture, deploy and replenish its defence capabilities.
Recent global conflicts have reinforced a critical lesson: military strength depends not just on advanced capabilities, but also on munitions depth and the ability to replenish them at scale. India must build resilient domestic supply chains and independently develop and manufacture technologies vital to its national security.At IG Defence, our ambition goes beyond individual products. We aim to build indigenous technologies, intellectual property and manufacturing infrastructure for the weapons systems of tomorrow. JWALA embodies our commitment to indigenous missile technology, while GRID Forge represents our vision for software-defined defence manufacturing. Together, they will form the foundation of a next-generation manufacturing ecosystem. Our partnership with the Government of Andhra Pradesh is an important step towards realising this vision.
India must move beyond being a buyer or assembler of defence technologies to becoming their developer, owner and manufacturer.”
The initiative aligns with the Government of India’s vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India, while supporting the broader objective of establishing India as a globally competitive defence technology and manufacturing hub.Through indigenous product development, advanced manufacturing infrastructure and software-defined industrial systems, IG Defence aims to contribute to a new generation of Indian defence capabilities. The ambition is not simply to build another defence factory. It is to build an indigenous defence manufacturing ecosystem that can develop the technologies of tomorrow, manufacture at scale and strengthen India’s strategic autonomy.
IG Defence — For the Nation, With Precision.

morning.title: Defence Secretary Raises Question Over Tejas Mk2 Future
morning.text:
India’s Tejas Mk2 fighter jet is still on the cards for the Indian Air Force but the actual procurement will depend on its performance following its first flight, and whether other procurement programmes can fully satisfy the IAF’s fighter needs. Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh has said the government will re-evaluate the programme once it takes to the skies, which is currently scheduled for mid-2027.
“As of now, it is still part of their plans. Let’s see once it flies in the middle of next year we’ll see whether we take an AoN for it and take it forward in the procurement cycle or whether some of the other programmes that we have mentioned, including the MRFA programme, is adequate and therefore we don’t need to sort of pursue that route,” Singh told ANI at the National Security Summit 3.0 in New Delhi on November 16.
While the programme does continue to be supported, it is clear that Singh has indicated that the government may re-evaluate the need for the Tejas Mk2 once it is developed.
An Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) is an important first step in the defence procurement process in India, without which the Tejas Mk2 cannot enter the procurement cycle for an IAF order. Singh made it clear that the government would want to look at the aircraft first.
The first flight, due around mid-2027, will be an important milestone. The prototype will have to prove it can fly and meets the IAF’s requirements.
The government will also consider the Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft (MRFA) programme to procure 114 foreign origin fighters. If it can deliver a good capability then the government may look to not procure the Tejas Mk2.
However, they are not necessarily a direct replacement for each other. The Tejas Mk2 is meant to provide an indigenous medium weight fighter capability, while the MRFA is looking to meet the IAF’s need for extra multirole fighters. Cost, timelines, availability, maintenance and role will all play a part.
The programme is being developed by the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA). It is expected that production will be led by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) under the current public sector model. However, Singh has emphasised that it will be developed using a spiral development approach. This means it will be continuously upgraded with lots of input from the private sector and MSMEs.
The IAF previously indicated it would require around 120 Tejas Mk2s. However, this should not be taken as an order. The government has indicated that a decision will be made once the prototype has been developed.

morning.title: Kerch Bridge Struck For The Second Time In Less Than 24 Hours: Russia
morning.text:
Ukraine has launched a second attack on the Kerch Bridge in less than 24 hours. The latest strike on Vladimir Putin’s prized span linking occupied Crimean with Russia was confirmed by the Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov.

“The enemy attacked the Crimean Bridge again,” Aksyonov wrote on Telegram at about 1:34 a.m. local time on Tuesday. “Currently, traffic is suspended.”

“We ask residents and visitors of Crimea to refrain from traveling towards the bridge and to take into account any restrictions when planning their routes,” he added. “We will provide further updates on the situation. Please remember to only trust official sources of information.”

Videos have emerged on social media purporting to show explosions and fire from the latest attack. In particular, one clip shows an explosion in what appears to be the same part of the bridge that was hit before and the bridge losing its shape. However, the poor nature of imagery makes it hard to discern its authenticity or the outcome of the strike if it is indeed real.

So far, no Ukrainian officials have come forward to take credit for the second strike on the Kerch Bridge, which, as we suggested hours ago, would likely happen.

As we noted in our story about the earlier first attack, the extent of the damage from that incident remains unclear, but there were very visible signs of the main road span on the Kerch side of the bridge having been damaged.

Footage broadcast on Russian television first showed significant damage to the crossing. The main road span looks to have sustained a direct hit to its arch, with visible deformation of the structure.

Meanwhile, satellite imagery confirmed signs of damage to the bridge following the first attack, including around the arch of the road crossing, consistent with what we can see in the Russian television report. The imagery also appeared to show dark marks, possibly scorch marks, at the opposite end of the main road span, although these may not be related to the initial attack.

There are indications that the damaged arch was tilted 4.9 degrees after the first attack. Such damage could severely limit the loads the span can safely carry.

The Monday attack marked the first time in more than a year Ukraine struck the bridge after three previous attacks damaged it. The bridge has remained a top target for Ukrainian forces. Beyond its enormous symbolic value as a signature infrastructure project associated with Putin, it provides a critical road and rail connection for moving military personnel, equipment, and supplies between mainland Russia and occupied Crimea.

This is a developing story.

UPDATE: 8:14 PM EST –

Financial Times is reporting that Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko says preliminary reports are that Russian ballistic missiles have hit the northern and southern bridges in Ukraine’s capital.

“Russia has intensified its strikes on Kyiv’s bridges over the Dnipro river in recent weeks,” the publication’s Christopher Miller noted on X. “Ukraine responded last night by hitting the Kerch bridge in occupied Crimea. It seems Moscow decided tonight it would further escalate attacks on the crucial expanses connecting Kyiv and the eastern and western halves of Ukraine.”

“Something new appears to have shifted technologically and/or tactically for Ukraine being able to successfully strike the Kerch Bridge,” TWZ editor-in-chief Tyler Rogoway noted on X. “Unclear what it is, but there has been a new construct here we will probably soon learn about.”

The strikes took place even though, as we previously reported, Ukraine has experienced new disruptions in service from the SpaceX Starshield satellite communications system.

UPDATE: 10:23 PM EST –

Sevastopol residents wanting to head to Russia are being urged not to use the Kerch Bridge.

“The Ukrainian Armed Forces have once again attacked the Crimean Bridge,” Mikhail Razvozhayev, the Russian-installed governor of Sevastopol, said on Telegram. “Traffic has been suspended. I am in constant contact with the Head of the Republic of Crimea, Sergey Valerievich Aksyonov, and we are coordinating our actions and jointly working on all necessary decisions.”

“For those who were planning to leave Sevastopol and travel to mainland Russia via the bridge tonight or this morning, please refrain from traveling for now,” he added. “More information will be available tomorrow morning.”

morning.text: Mumbai: Net dollar purchases in the forwards market more than halved through October from the previous month to about $17 billion as targeted regulatory curbs on hedging took effect, building stability in the value of the rupee that surged from the end of the month to anchor a stunning revival of overseas interest in India-listed growth assets.The Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), brought in to dissuade unnecessary currency hedging amid a haemorrhage that even record hauls from forex-inflow programmes couldn't seemingly staunch, immediately reduced dollar purchases in the forward market in October to $49 billion from $76 billion in September, CCIL data showed.135906856Dollar sales, meanwhile, reduced to $32 billion from $41 billion, marking a broader reduction in dollar demand that stood in sharp relief against a steady climb in the dollar index over the past four weeks. The dollar climbed 1.5% against a basket of six heavily traded currencies through this period, while the removal of state oil retailers' demand from the spot market and absence of unnecessary hedging provided the spot rupee the cushion it needed to draw in overseas funds.Read more: Indian equities ride global AI trade unwind: Is D-Street back on foreign investors' radar? BNP Paribas answers"Overall hedging has gone down after FERR and things have got more stringent. So, hedging happens only for what is required," said Sajal Gupta, head of forex and commodities at Nuvama. "Importers are hedging on a short-term basis while exporters still feel that the weakness in the rupee may reappear and are holding back on hedging."Read more: Ahead of Market: 10 things that will decide stock market action on TuesdayHedging demand over the last few years has contributed to increased dollar demand, with importers hedging more and exporters hedging less.The rupee has recovered since mid-October, after touching near 97 levels last month. It closed at 93.92 on Monday, and has gained more than 3% from its record low levels.'Weakness Bias'The gap between forward dollar purchases and sales widened to $233 billion in FY26 from $97 billion in FY24, indicating a substantial increase in net dollar demand arising from hedging activity. Importers increasingly hedged amid expectations of sustained rupee deprecation, while exporters reduced their dollar sales, thus increasing dollar demand.FERR increased importer hedging costs by requiring banks to park 20% of the rupee value of eligible forward contracts with the RBI in non-interest-bearing cash reserves. This raises banks' funding and opportunity costs, which are passed on to importers through higher hedging charges, making forward dollar purchases more expensive."However, the effectiveness of FERR will depend on how long importer hedging remains curtailed. If the expectation of continued rupee depreciation persists, then importer hedging could pick up," said Gaura Sengupta, chief economist, IDFC First Bank.

morning.title: US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China
morning.text:
The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations.

The interim final rule [PDF] containing the new regulations says they’re needed “to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”

Similar language can be found in previous US bans on sales of GPUs and other advanced tech to China, which Washington fears will use advanced tech to improve its military capabilities.

US authorities understood that export bans wouldn’t prevent Chinese entities from renting GPUs housed elsewhere. So from 2021 to 2024, Washington introduced a series of regulations that required US-based clouds to make sure they didn’t serve Chinese customers.

No such obligation existed for cloud operators elsewhere, which created a market for resources that Chinese customers could access from afar. It is widely felt that datacenter building booms in Malaysia and Thailand, both of which are generally on good terms with China, aimed to cater to Middle Kingdom customers who wanted to rent GPUs they could not import.

Megapseed – whose former employee Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and may have been a Chinese intelligence asset – built datacenters in Malaysia and was suspected of catering largely to offshore customers.

Neil Shah, vice president of research at analyst firm Counterpoint, said the new rules shift the regulatory burden of complying with export controls from hardware manufacturers to cloud operators.

“Data center operators in hubs such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia will now face massive ‘Know Your Customer's Workload’ requirements,” he told The Register by email, likening it to the KYC restrictions imposed on financial services firms. “They must prove to US regulators that their compute is not being funneled back to embargoed nations, or risk losing their own access to US silicon.”

He feels the new rules represent “a severe short-term compute bottleneck for Chinese tech giants” and “a massive long-term catalyst for decoupling.”

“Washington is forcing domestic capital and engineering talent to double down on full-stack sovereign alternatives, accelerating ecosystems like Huawei's Ascend.”

Shah’s observation came days after Alibaba decided to spin out its T-Head chip design unit, which it described as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China.” That description suggests Alibaba doesn’t think T-Head has strong prospects of selling its wares outside China.

It remains to be seen if the new BIS rules will slow datacenter development across Asia and Brazil. All five nations the US has regulated are all enjoying the economic impact of the AI boom. They’re also trying to manage its impact. Singapore limits datacenter construction, as befits a tiny and resource-constrained island nation. Malaysia is very much open for business but has introduced increasingly strict building codes and requirements to minimize energy and water consumption. Thailand recently introduced new regulations that new builds of large datacenters must take place in designated industrial zones. Indonesia also has strong regulations but is not currently a major datacenter hub.

Brazil requires datacenter operators to reserve at least 10 percent of capacity for local users, suggesting some operators are more interested in offshore customers.

Interestingly, the new BIS rules don’t impact infrastructure used for “commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.”

Chinese e-tailers operate at vast scale and have already attracted regulatory attention in Europe and the USA. Asian and Brazilian datacenter operators therefore probably do not see the likes of Temu and Alibaba as a lifeline, but might see a role as regional hosts for outfits like Amazon or Meta. ®

First F-15EXs Arrive At Kadena Air Base In Japan, 25 Now Delivered To The USAF
morning.text:
The U.S. Air Force now has two F-15EX Eagle II fighters permanently forward-deployed at Kadena Air Base on the Japanese island of Okinawa. The 18th Wing has been awaiting the arrival of F-15EXs as replacements for its retired F-15C/D Eagles for years now. This milestone also highlights the continued expansion of the overall Air Force Eagle II fleet, which has now grown to 25 jets.

The 18th Wing announced that its first F-15EXs had touched down at Kadena yesterday. Prime contractor Boeing confirmed today that those jets were the 22nd and 23rd Eagle IIs produced (EX22 and EX23) in posts across its social media accounts. The expectation is that 36 F-15EXs will eventually be based in Japan, with 18 each assigned to the 44th and 67th Fighter Squadrons.

Boeing also confirmed to TWZ directly today that 25 F-15EXs have been delivered to the Air Force. This includes all of the jets in the first and second production lots. Lot 3 deliveries are now underway. The total Air Force Eagle IIs fleet is now set to reach 267 airframes, roughly double what the program of record was in 2025.

EX22, the first Japan-bound Eagle II, had left Boeing’s plant in St. Louis in September and traveled first to Portland Air National Guard Base in Oregon. The base is collocated with Portland International Airport and is home to the Oregon Air National Guard’s 142nd Wing, the first unit to fly combat-coded F-15EXs. The 142nd has been central to coordinating and preparing the way for the deployment of Eagle IIs to Kadena.

In the lead up to this weekend’s deployment, “operators from the 67th Fighter Squadron traveled to Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, and Portland Air National Guard Base, Oregon, to maintain flying proficiency and complete aircraft qualification training in preparation for the aircraft’s arrival,” according to the 18th Wing’s press release. “Maintenance personnel from the 18th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron also spent years preparing for the transition, coordinating with Boeing and Air Force teams at Eglin and Portland to develop and maintain technical proficiency. They additionally supported F-15E operations at Seymour-Johnson Air Force Base, North Carolina, and Mountain Home Air Force Base, Idaho, gaining valuable experience while supporting the broader fighter enterprise.”

The Air Force began a phased withdrawal of F-15C/Ds from Kadena in November 2022, but did not initially confirm what those aircraft would be replaced by. TWZ was the first to report in 2024 that the decision had officially been made to forward-base F-15EXs in Japan permanently through an interview with Col. Michael Kosderka, then commander of the 142nd Wing.

In the interim, the Air Force had been making rotational deployments of F-16C/D Vipers, F-15E Strike Eagles, F-22 Raptors, and F-35 Joint Strike Fighters to the base in Japan to fill the resulting gaps in operational capacity left by the departed F-15C/Ds. Eagle II test jets had also previously traveled to Kadena on temporary deployments as part of exercises.

“Getting the F-15EX to Kadena is just the beginning,” Air Force Lt. Col. Ajay Dua, head of the 67th Fighter Squadron, said in a statement this weekend. “Now our focus shifts to integrating the aircraft into our flying operations, building experience as a squadron, and learning how to get the most out of its capabilities. It’s an exciting time to be part of the 67th Fighter Squadron.”

As we have previously written:

“The F-15EX will give U.S. forces in the Indo-Pacific a high-capacity platform that complements the fifth-generation F-22 and F-35. With its ability to carry large air-to-air and air-to-surface payloads, the Eagle II can serve as a long-range ‘missile truck,’ extending the reach and firepower of stealth aircraft operating closer to contested airspace. Its open-architecture systems also allow it to incorporate new sensors, weapons, and electronic warfare capabilities more readily than the aging F-15C/D fleet.”

“The aircraft’s value is also tied to its role in networked operations. Exercises such as Valiant Shield have demonstrated how the F-15EX can work with uncrewed aircraft like the MQ-28 Ghost Bat, pointing toward mixed formations in which crewed fighters provide weapons, sensing, and command-and-control capacity for autonomous wingmen. Operating from strategic locations such as Kadena, the Eagle II could help the Air Force generate more combat power across the vast Pacific while reducing the burden on its limited number of stealth fighters.”

The deployment of the first F-15EXs to Kadena also follows the appearance of conformal fuel tanks (CFT) on operational Eagle IIs assigned to the 142nd earlier this month. The F-15EX is designed to use the same CFTs as the F-15E, which can also be fitted to other jets in the extended Strike Eagle family. However, the Air Force initially decided against acquiring the tanks for use on combat-coded F-15EXs, ostensibly because of the focus on air-to-air combat applications for these jets.

Since then, the Eagle II’s mission requirements have continued to evolve, especially in the air-to-ground arena. The benefits CFTs offer can also be relevant during air-to-air combat missions. TWZ recently explored all of this in greater depth, writing, in part:

“Even just within the context of air-to-air missions, CFT-equipped F-15EXs would be particularly beneficial for supporting future operations in the Pacific. The inherent geography of the region means access to bases on the ground and tanker support could easily be limited. With CFTs, Eagle IIs would be able to operate further forward of tankers and be able to do so for longer periods of time, helping to extend patrol distances and total on-station time. Not having to carry drop tanks would also translate to more ordnance capacity on those sorties.”

The plan now for expanding the fielding of CFTs across the F-15EX fleet, including jets now being forward-deployed to Japan, is still not entirely clear.

Otherwise, “the arrival of the F-15EX at Kadena marks a significant milestone for American airpower in the Pacific,” Air Force Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, head of the 18th Wing, said in a statement yesterday. “These aircraft strengthen our ability to deter aggression, respond to emerging threats and defend Japan alongside our allies and partners. Their permanent presence at Kadena reinforces our commitment to the U.S.-Japan alliance and ensures we continue to bring advanced combat capabilities to one of the most strategically important regions in the world.”

While the start of permanent deployments of F-15EXs to Kadena is certainly a milestone, it does also highlight certain production and sustainment concerns. Boeing was originally supposed to have completed delivery of Lot 3 by early 2026, but experienced delays largely stemming from a labor strike in 2025. That, in turn, caused the schedule for sending jets to the 18th Wing to shift to the right.

Internal Pentagon reports have also warned about the growing need for the F-15EX program to address issues related to diminishing manufacturing sources and material shortages. All of this has raised questions about whether or not the Air Force will be able to keep to its longer-term schedules for fielding Eagle IIs to other units.

Still, with the first two F-15EXs now based at Kadena, combat-coded Eagle IIs now look set to increasingly leave their mark on the Western Pacific.

Contact the author: joe@twz.com

morning.title: California sues OpenAI for misleading public about AI safety
morning.text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI under the state's unfair competition and public nuisance laws, for allegedly misleading and endangering the public by deploying unsafe AI models.

The lawsuit [PDF], filed in California Superior Court, follows the compromise of Hugging Face's infrastructure and other cyber incidents OpenAI's experimental models caused when taking autonomous actions without authorization or supervision.

"While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents," said Attorney General Bonta.

At a press conference, Bonta added: "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public."

The legal salvo comes after Bonta in September sent OpenAI a letter seeking information about these agentic attacks. According to the complaint, "OpenAI failed to substantially comply" with the investigatory subpoena.

In August, 15 states led by Iowa – and excluding California – issued a joint demand for OpenAI to provide information about how its models hacked Hugging Face.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.

Bonta's office previously joined with Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings to urge OpenAI to do more for children's safety in light of reports that its models produced sexually inappropriate output. California did not, however, join the eight states that sued OpenAI in October over alleged misrepresentations about child safety. Florida and Texas have also made child safety claims.

Child safety plays well politically; California appears to be the first state to demand more accountability toward the general public.

Bonta's lawsuit, in a state that has largely accommodated the AI industry for the sake of economic benefits and political contributions, suggests that California officials may be more willing to bite the hand that feeds.

The many Democratic victories in the US midterm elections may also be a factor, as pundits feel voters swung to give lawmakers license to regulate the unpopular AI industry.

At his press conference, Bonta made sure to convey that he wants accountability without smothering the AI industry in costly regulation.

"Let me be clear," he said. "I believe in the technological and economic power of AI. If we're able to address these very high stakes safety issues, AI could lead to some of the most incredible improvements in the history of humankind."

AI is yet to deliver those incredible improvements. It has delivered deepfakes, huge quantities of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and the permissionless resale of past intellectual labor, plus high energy and RAM prices. As well as some productivity gains in certain areas like coding, albeit at an unknown cost to future job markets.

But as AI boosters insist, miracle drugs and endless vacations aren't far off … perhaps along with existential crises.

Katharine Trendacosta, director of policy and advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told The Register in an email that the EFF is glad to see state officials taking action against AI companies taking unreasonable risks with public safety.

"Several recent cybersecurity incidents at AI labs could have been prevented or substantially mitigated by adhering to longstanding cybersecurity best practices, such as proper sandboxing, monitoring, and logging," said Trendacosta.

"AI agents can be useful tools when deployed appropriately, with adequate safeguards designed to mitigate the risks. Companies should carefully consider the risks of every use case, including the consequences, reversibility, and sensitivity of any action an agent is used for." ®

morning.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
morning.text:
A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents."

Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.

The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates.

morning.title: Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach
morning.text:
Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data.

"Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register.

According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint.

This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade.

The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents.

Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said.

“We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue."

Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years.

Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected.

The Register will update this story as we learn more about the breach.®

morning.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
morning.text:
One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.

A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward.

Finding the centers

The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.
